function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to help you prepare the files you need, but I don’t have the ability to run `git` commands or write directly to your local filesystem from here.  
What I can do is:

1. **Generate the contents** of the Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub‑Actions workflow that you can copy into the repository.  
2. **Explain how to add, commit, and push** those files once you’ve pasted them into the correct locations.

Below are the suggested files based on a typical Node.js “welcome” application. Feel free to tweak the values (e.g., image tags, ports) to match your exact setup.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` gives a small, production‑ready base image.  
> * `npm ci --only=production` installs only production dependencies, keeping the image lean.  
> * Exposes port `3000`, which is the common default for many Node apps (adjust if your app uses a different port).  

If you prefer to use one of the images listed in the tool signature (`python:3.x-slim`), replace the `FROM` line accordingly, but keep in mind that a Node app needs a Node base image.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` (or whatever you prefer):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/your-org/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update with your registry & tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if needed
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # External port
    targetPort: 3000          # Container port
```

> **Key points**  
> * `replicas: 3` – adjust based on load expectations.  
> * `image:` – replace with the actual image you’ll push to your registry (GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, etc.).  
> * `type: LoadBalancer` – exposes the service externally; switch to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP` if you’re running locally or inside a private cluster.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }},ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
        cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache

    - name: Clean up cache
      run: rm -rf /tmp/.buildx-cache
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the image using Docker Buildx (supports multi‑platform builds).  
> * Pushes two tags: a SHA‑based tag for reproducibility and a `latest` tag.  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication to GitHub Container Registry.  

Make sure the repository has the `GHCR` scope enabled for the token (this is automatic for `GITHUB_TOKEN`).

---

## 4. Adding, Committing, and Pushing

Once you’ve copied the above files into the appropriate paths:

```bash
# Add the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repository
git push origin main
```

If you’re working on a feature branch, replace `main` with your branch name and merge later.

---

### Quick Checklist

| Step | What to do | Command / Action |
|------|------------|------------------|
| 1 | Clone repo | `git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` |
| 2 | Copy Dockerfile, `k8s-deployment.yaml`, and workflow into repo | Paste the contents above |
| 3 | Add files | `git add ...` |
| 4 | Commit | `git commit -m "..."` |
| 5 | Push | `git push origin main` |

That’s it! Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically build and publish your Docker image whenever you push to `main`. If you run into any errors (e.g., missing permissions, wrong image names), let me know and I can help troubleshoot.
